title: p99-p95 tail latency deep dive with Meridian AI
summary: Deep technical discussion about observed p95/p99 spikes in Meridian's chat API. Main causes explored: KV-cache misses and warmup, batching policies causing head-of-line blocking, network hops from VPC peering and NAT gateways, and quantization inference variance. Redwood SE outlined mitigations: aggressive prefix caching, dynamic batching limits per route, prioritized streaming lanes, and dedicated capacity with private routing. Agreed next steps: Meridian to provide sample traffic traces and prompt set; Redwood to run KV-cache-focused benchmark and share preliminary Dedicated pricing and security docs.
next_steps: Redwood (Priya): run kv-cache-focused benchmark on 8xA100 within 3 business days and share results
Meridian (Carlos): export and share 24h request traces + representative prompts by 2027-10-18
Redwood (Jordan): share Dedicated pricing range + security (SOC2/KMS) doc links
Schedule: 2-hour on-prem pilot planning session (TBD week of 10/25)
action_items: Priya Shah: setup benchmark job (kv-cache emphasis) and attach latency histograms
Carlos Vega: provide examples of tail requests and percent token lengths, include streaming vs non-streaming flags
Tom Liu: confirm whether client uses HTTP streaming or polling for chat messages
Jordan Miles: send Redwood security pack and sample SLA language
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55m
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Miguel Ortega (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Meridian CTO), Aisha Khan (Meridian SRE), Tom Liu (ML Eng), Sofia Park (Product)

[00:00] Jordan: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick goal for today - we want to zero in on your p95/p99 tail spikes and figure out where the biggest wins are. Priya and Miguel from the SE team are here. Carlos, do you want to kick off with measured symptoms?

[00:17] Carlos: yeah thanks jordan. so we've been seeing occasional p99s in the 800-1200ms range for chat completions when our median is around 120-160ms. it's kinda bursty - looks like at certain times the p95 climbs too. it's mostly for the streaming path but some non-streaming endpoints also spike. we instrumented spans but it's fuzzy.

[00:36] Priya: got it. couple quick q's - are you using prefix caching or any KV cache on your side? and are clients using HTTP streaming or long-polling websocket?

[00:46] Carlos: we recently added an internal prefix cache for some intents but not the LLM kv cache. clients - mixed; mobile uses HTTP streaming, server-side uses gRPC streaming for the enterprise product.

[01:05] Miguel: (murmur) okay that mix explains a lot, since streaming lanes behave differently in our runtime.

[01:12] Tom: to add - we also saw higher tails when we hit scale-up events (autoscaler creating new nodes) - cold warmup seems to add 200-300ms occasionally.

[01:25] Priya: yeah cold start warmup plus kv-cache cold misses are the two usual suspects. i want to walk through the request path and common latency contributors: tokenization, KV lookup, attention kernel execution, device-host sync, and network hops - esp over VPC peering/NAT.

[01:44] Jordan: and also important - streaming changes when we flush tokens earlier, there's overhead per fragment. so p99 on streaming is not directly comparable to non-streaming.

[02:02] Aisha: question - we run in our AWS VPC and connect to Redwood Private via VPC peering + a managed NAT for some calls to object storage. could NAT be adding jitter?

[02:12] Priya: yes NAT and additional network hops (like S3 for prompt assets or model artifacts) can add nondeterministic latency. we often see 10-40ms of jitter per extra hop, but it can be worse if routes hit transitive peering that has transient packet loss.

[02:30] Carlos: interesting. we do have prompt assets pulled from S3 on first request - could be correlated with cold requests.

[02:38] Miguel: exactly. another thing - KV cache in the runtime is per-worker and benefits from warm request routing. if requests are scattered across many workers (due to round-robin LB) the effective cache hit rate drops and p99 blows up.

[02:56] Jordan: do you shard clients across many small pods, or use fewer large instances?

[03:02] Tom: we historically used many small pods to scale quickly; recently experimenting with larger ones but haven't tuned batching.

[03:10] Priya: okay that explains head-of-line blocking too: with many small pods, large batches can form unpredictably causing one request to wait for others. recommended is dynamic batching with max batch latency and size per route. also prioritized lanes for streaming so interactive tokens are not held up.

[03:35] Carlos: can you explain prioritized lanes? we haven't heard that term before.

[03:39] Priya: short version - separate worker queues by priority. streaming/incremental responses get a fast lane with strict batch size limits (often batch_size 1-4 but low latency), non-streaming completions go to a throughput lane with larger batch sizes. the runtime routes by policy, so you get throughput without penalizing interactive tail latency.

[03:58] Aisha: is that a config we can set in Redwood Dedicated / Private? or is it platform side?

[04:05] Miguel: it's configurable - on Dedicated we expose route-level batching and lane configs in the console. on Private we can ship the same config via the control plane. note there's a tradeoff: more lanes = more GPU underutilization unless autoscaler policies are tuned.

[04:22] Tom: what about quantization - we saw different latency profiles between int8 and fp16 on our tests; sometimes int8 was faster, sometimes fp16 was more predictable.

[04:33] Priya: quantization tradeoffs are real. int8 can reduce memory bandwidth and sometimes reduce latency, but it can increase CPU overhead for dequant/quant ops and affect kernel selection. the runtime has quantization-friendly kernels but they depend on model arch and sequence length. for p99 predictability, fp16 often wins unless we optimize kernels for int8.

[04:56] Jordan: and we should remember model compilation - when a model is JIT-compiled to a specific kernel set, the first few requests can be slower. we precompile on Dedicated to avoid that.

[05:08] Carlos: ok so precompile + warm KV cache + prioritized streaming lanes + tune batching. what's the impact of network hops again - if we move to Private in our VPC does that remove most of the jitter?

[05:21] Priya: it reduces a lot, yes. Private deployment with colocated inference and route traffic inside the VPC avoids public NATs. but you still need to watch cross-AZ hops and load-balancer config. also, on-prem has different failure modes like noisy neighbors on shared NICs.

[05:40] Sofia: question - do you have metrics that show the p99 delta attributed to KV miss vs network vs kernel variance?

[05:48] Miguel: we do in our internal harness - flame charts and span attribution. typical split we see: 30-45% kernel/execution variability, 25-35% network/hop jitter, 20-30% cache misses and warmup, remaining is tokenization and orchestration. but this depends heavily on sequence length distribution.

[06:12] Carlos: our sequences are very variable - median 50 tokens but tail 600-900 tokens for some workflows. that probably aggravates tail.

[06:22] Priya: yep long sequences amplify kernel variability and KV cache pressure. also batching policies that don't consider sequence length can bunch long and short requests causing long-tail at serving. we recommend size-based batching - group by token-length buckets.

[06:40] Jordan: can you walk us through a typical request trace from your users that hit p99? just narrate steps and timings.

[06:46] Carlos: sure - user triggers chat, client opens streaming, initial prompt fetch from S3 (if not cached) - ~120ms. tokenization + first token generation 80ms. subsequent tokens come in streaming bursts, but at around token 120 we sometimes hit a model-host rotation because of autoscaler causing a 300ms pause, then kv-cache miss for a repeated prefix (we don't cache it) adds 200ms and tokens resume. cumulative effect hits 1100ms for some requests.

[07:28] Priya: that chain is useful. two immediate wins: prefetch prompts to avoid S3 on cold path, and pin long-running chat sessions to a worker to improve KV cache locality (session affinity).

[07:42] Aisha: session affinity - does that hurt load distribution?

[07:45] Miguel: it can, but we do affinity with soft TTLs; plus routing policy can prioritize affinity for streaming sessions and fall back after idle timeout. it's a tradeoff versus cache-hit improvement.

[07:58] Tom: you mentioned KV cache persistence across restarts - is that possible in Private/On-prem?

[08:03] Priya: the runtime supports persistent KV cache via memory-backed snapshots or external redis-like stores for cold restarts. snapshots persist to local NVMe to speed warmup. external stores add a network hop but can be worth it for large clusters.

[08:18] Carlos: hmm NVMe snapshots sound promising. do you have numbers on warmup times with snapshots?

[08:24] Miguel: ballpark: without snapshot, warmup for a large model + KV can be 20-45s for full cold. with NVMe snapshot we often see warmups <5s to reach stable hit rates, depends on IO throughput.

[08:40] Jordan: let's talk about benchmarking methodology. Priya, recommended bench plan?

[08:44] Priya: run two passes: 1) synthetic steady-state with a representative token distribution to measure median/p95 under tuned batching/lanes; 2) kv-cache stress: randomized sessions with affinity toggled to measure hit-rate vs tail. capture histograms, spans, and perf counters for kernel variance. we'll also run streaming vs non-streaming comparisons and toggle quantization.

[09:08] Carlos: we can provide prompts and traffic - how do we give them to you?

[09:12] Jordan: Carlos - ideally a gzipped trace with timestamps, tokens per request, streaming flag, and any user session id. we can upload to the shared bucket or a secure link.

[09:23] Aisha: security question - if we use Private, how do you handle KMS and keys? we need customer-managed keys.

[09:30] Priya: we support KMS integration - on Private we can integrate with your cloud KMS or HSM for encryption at rest and for signing model checksums. we'll share the SOC2/ISO pack.

[09:41] Tom: ok great. pricing question - rough estimate for Dedicated vs Private?

[09:46] Jordan: we'll send an initial pricing range in the deck; dedicated is usually a reserved capacity commit with monthly cost and burst allowances. Private has platform/license + infra. i'll attach a preliminary ballpark after this call.

[10:00] Carlos: another gotcha - our edge users are in eu-west with single az. cross-az traffic to a us-east Redwood hosted endpoint added 40-60ms and spikes sometimes. any recs?

[10:10] Priya: run inference regionally or use Dedicated pools in region. if that's not possible, use streaming with smaller fragments to reduce buffer time; though that increases per-token overhead. it's tradeoffs.

[10:23] Miguel: also check if your VPC peering forces traffic through transit gateways - that can add tens to hundreds of ms when overloaded.

[10:33] Sofia: question - what observability do we get? token-level latency? per-route p99?

[10:38] Priya: Redwood Console gives per-route histograms, token-level breakdown (tokenize vs kv vs kernel vs network), tracing, and correlation with rollout versions. we can populate dashboards for your routes.

[10:51] Jordan: let's go through a few hypothetical mitigations and their expected impact - priya, you want to lead?

[10:55] Priya: sure: 1) prefetch prompt assets: reduces cold path S3 hits - up to 100-200ms reduction on cold requests. 2) session affinity for streaming: can improve KV hit by 20-40% on sessions and reduce p99 substantially. 3) prioritized streaming lanes with batch limits: reduces streaming p99 by moving interactive traffic out of large throughput batches. 4) NVMe snapshot for KV: reduces warmup from tens of seconds to single-digit seconds. 5) region/dedicated pools: eliminate public NAT jitter and cross-region latency. each has cost tradeoffs - e.g., affinity + many reserved workers increases GPU utilization.

[11:36] Carlos: for the prioritized lanes, what's the typical GPU utilization impact? we can't afford 30% inefficiency.

[11:42] Miguel: depends on traffic mix. often it's 5-15% utilization delta if you size lanes carefully and autoscaler allows burst pooling. the Optimize product can simulate utilization given your traffic mix.

[11:55] Tom: when you say Optimize simulates, does that mean you run a synthetic model of our distribution?

[11:59] Priya: we can ingest your traces and run the cost/latency simulation to recommend batch/quantization profiles. we'll include that as part of the POC.

[12:09] Aisha: if we move to Private on-prem, are there extra config steps for NVMe snapshots? our infra team wants to know.

[12:16] Miguel: it's straightforward - the runtime writes checkpointed KV pages to a configured NVMe mount. we provide the operator helm chart credentials and some tuning knobs for IO concurrency.

[12:28] Jordan: quick note - sometimes transcription incorrectly calls our product "Redwood Dedicate" in your docs; ignore that - it's Redwood Dedicated.

[12:35] (laughter)

[12:38] Carlos: noted. couple of quick, slightly fuzzy items - 1) do you support gRPC streaming with chunked partial tokens? 2) does prefix caching respect privacy rules if we want to evict after N requests?

[12:49] Priya: 1) yes gRPC streaming supported; chunked tokens are handled; we have per-chunk ack to avoid head-of-line. 2) prefix cache has TTL/LSR eviction and explicit invalidation APIs so you can evict sensitive prefixes immediately.

[13:05] Tom: what about quantization regressions - do you run evals for quality drift?

[13:10] Priya: yes, Redwood has an eval pipeline - before we recommend int8 we run your evals on a holdout prompt set to detect quality regression. we tie alerts to rollouts if quality drops.

[13:24] Carlos: ok this is good. can you give a recommended POC scope?

[13:30] Jordan: recommended POC: 2-week bench on Dedicated or Private trial: 1) run the kv-cache stress and streaming vs non-streaming tests; 2) tune batching and lanes; 3) run quantization A/B; 4) observe p95/p99 improvements and recommend configs.

[13:45] Aisha: timeline?

[13:48] Jordan: we can start benchmarks within 3 business days once we have traces and access; initial findings in 5 business days.

[13:56] Miguel: we'll also include a doc with mitigations prioritized by expected p99 reduction per unit cost.

[14:03] Carlos: perfect. one more - do you have guidance on client-side backpressure? our mobile clients sometimes retransmit making load spikes.

[14:13] Priya: use client-side jitter/randomized retry with exponential backoff, and prefer streaming to reduce retransmit windows. telemetry on client retry rates helps too.

[14:25] (short pauses, background typing)

[14:45] Jordan: okay let's move to concrete next steps and action items (recap). Priya?

[14:50] Priya: recap: Redwood runs KV-cache benchmark, Meridian provides traces and prompt set, Redwood sends pricing and security docs, schedule follow-up to review bench. action items in the notes.

[14:59] Jordan: thanks everyone. we'll shoot the benchmark plan and an upload link to Carlos after this.
notes_footer: Call ended ~16:55 UTC. Recording and transcript uploaded to shared folder. References: benchmark-template.csv, redwood-dedicated-pricing.pdf, redwood-security-pack.zip.
